questiontext.text: Which representation lets any general (multiway) tree be stored as a binary tree?

feedback.text: Correct — first child goes left, next sibling goes right.
No — that stores a complete binary tree in an array, not a general tree as binary.
No — that is a general graph representation, not this tree mapping.
No — threading reuses NULL pointers for traversal; it does not convert general to binary.

generalfeedback.text: The left-child, right-sibling scheme reuses a binary node's two pointers as "first child" and "next sibling", encoding an arbitrary-degree tree.

questiontext.text: In the left-child, right-sibling encoding, a node's left pointer refers to its ______.

feedback.text: Correct — the left pointer points to the node's first child.
No — the next sibling is stored in the right pointer.
No — the encoding stores first child and next sibling, not parent.
No — it points to the first child; later children are reached via sibling links.

generalfeedback.text: Left = first child, right = next sibling. Descending left then chaining right visits all children of a node.

questiontext.text: In the left-child, right-sibling encoding, a node's right pointer refers to its ______.

feedback.text: Correct — the right pointer chains to the next sibling.
No — the first child is stored in the left pointer.
No — parent links are not part of this encoding.

answer.text: Right child in the original general tree

feedback.text: No — general-tree nodes have no fixed "right child"; the pointer holds the next sibling.

generalfeedback.text: Siblings form a right-linked chain, so a node of any degree needs only two pointers.

questiontext.text: The left-child, right-sibling mapping between forests/general trees and binary trees is best described as a ______.

feedback.text: Correct — every forest maps to exactly one binary tree and back.
No — the mapping loses no information and is fully reversible.
No — it applies to trees of arbitrary degree and to forests.
No — balance is irrelevant to the encoding.

generalfeedback.text: The encoding is a bijection: a forest of general trees corresponds to exactly one binary tree, and the process reverses uniquely.

questiontext.text: Any general tree or forest can be represented as a binary tree using the left-child, right-sibling scheme.

feedback.text: Correct — the encoding works for trees of any degree and for forests.
It can — this is a standard bijection between forests and binary trees.

questiontext.text: In the left-child, right-sibling encoding, a node's right pointer stores its first child.

feedback.text: No — the right pointer stores the next sibling; the first child is on the left.
Correct — right = next sibling, left = first child.

questiontext.text: In the left-child, right-sibling representation, the right pointer stores a node's next ______.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about the left-child, right-sibling representation are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: A node's first child becomes its left pointer

feedback.text: Yes — first child goes left.

answer.text: It is a bijection between forests and binary trees

feedback.text: Yes — the mapping is one-to-one and reversible.

answer.text: It only works when every node has at most two children

feedback.text: No — it works for arbitrary degree; that is its purpose.

answer.text: A node's next sibling becomes its left pointer

feedback.text: No — the next sibling becomes the right pointer.

generalfeedback.text: First child = left, next sibling = right; the scheme handles any degree and is a reversible bijection with binary trees.
